description:
We’re a homeschooling family of five (two parents and three kids) doing our first NASA Space Apps Challenge together. We think hackathons are an awesome way to learn: you pick a real problem, dig into real NASA data, and build something in a weekend.
We’re a family-only team, so we’re not looking for new members. We’re excited to meet everyone at the Princeton site and see what other teams build!
summary:
Two Cameras, One Calendar harmonizes NASA's two fire cameras into one burning activity calendar. Satellites have flagged fire hot spots for over twenty years, but the older camera, MODIS, is aging, and the newer VIIRS sees many small fires MODIS misses. Stitched together, the record jumps when the camera changes, as if fire had surged.

Learning from ten shared years (2012 to 2021), we found seasonal conversion numbers where the data support them and simpler ones for thin records, then put the available monthly records since November 2000 on one scale wherever a conversion holds. Tested on years held out, a typical month in Argentina lands within 9.5% of what MODIS counted, and within 25% in all 71 countries with a lot of fire. In years we could compare, 63 of 65 busy countries peak after 2021 when stitched; on VIIRS's scale, 9 do.

Our web app lists 235 countries and territories on an interactive globe, with a burning calendar, each country's latest available month against its historical median, and a monthly CSV download. A connector lets AI chat apps that support connectors (MCP) ask the same record; a volunteer page asks: fire, or something else? Responders, scientists and land managers can better tell an unusual season from a change of camera.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

The problem. Satellites have watched for fire from space since 2000. Their heat-sensing cameras flag a "hot spot" wherever a patch of ground is much hotter than the land around it. NASA's older camera, MODIS (on the Terra and Aqua satellites), holds the long record. The newer camera, VIIRS (on the Suomi NPP and NOAA-20 satellites), sees the ground in squares about 375 meters wide instead of about 1 kilometer, so it catches many small fires MODIS misses. MODIS is nearing the end of its working life, and VIIRS carries the record forward. Stitch the two together and the record jumps where the camera changes. In Argentina, the stitched record makes 2022 look like by far the biggest year: 89,310 against an earlier biggest year of 45,295. Most of that jump is sharper eyes, not more fire.

What we count. A hot spot detection is a square of ground about 5 km across where a camera flagged heat on one day. One big fire makes many detections, so these are counts of detections, not of fires or of land burned. We keep what NASA labels as likely vegetation fire.

How we harmonize. For each country and each month of the year, we take the ten years we learn from, 2012 to 2021, when both cameras were flying (they still are). We add up everything MODIS counted in that month across those years and divide by everything VIIRS counted in the same months. That gives a conversion number. Argentina, August: 62,467 ÷ 169,528 = 0.37. Where the data support it, a country gets twelve numbers, one per month, because the gap between the cameras changes with the seasons: in Argentina, MODIS counts about 37 for every 100 of VIIRS's in August, and about 24 in November. A thinner record gets one number for the whole year, or borrows a curve shared across countries, and where there is too little fire to convert, the page says so plainly. Of the 235 places listed, 90 have twelve numbers, 73 have one, 15 use the shared curve, and 57 have too little to convert. Multiply a VIIRS count by its month's number to estimate what MODIS would have counted; divide a MODIS count by it to estimate what VIIRS would have counted. The calendar opens on VIIRS's scale, because VIIRS is the camera going forward, and a switch shows MODIS's scale.

How we know it works. We hold one year out, here 2017, and work out the twelve numbers from the other nine years. Then we translate the held-out year and compare it with what MODIS really counted. October 2017: VIIRS counted 6,035; times October's number, 0.2873, gives 1,734; MODIS counted 1,921. That is 9.7% low. We do that for every usable month of every shared year: 119 months in Argentina. A typical month (the median: half landed closer, half further) lands within 9.5%, and nine months in ten within about 30%. Without harmonizing, VIIRS reads about 3.5 times what MODIS counts in a typical Argentine month. Beyond Argentina, in all 71 countries with a lot of fire (where MODIS, the older camera, counts a median of at least 50 detections a month in the learning years), a typical month lands within 25%, and the middle country within about 12%. The test measures agreement with MODIS, the one camera with real counts in both eras; it does not say which camera is closer to what happened on the ground. A second AI model family recounted these numbers on its own.

The months that miss teach us something too. January 2017 came out about 40% low. That summer, after a drought, large wildfires swept the Pampas (NASA's Earth Observatory reported on them on January 5, 2017). Big fires are the kind MODIS catches well, so the usual gap likely did not hold.

A smarter version, built and tested. It also sorts VIIRS's hot spots into seven bands by fire power (how much heat a fire gives off), because MODIS is more likely to catch the strong ones: about 4 in 100 of the faintest, about 57 in 100 of the strongest. With each test year left out of the country's monthly numbers, Argentina goes from 9.5% to 7.0%. Of the 71 countries, 51 improve by more than one percentage point, 19 change by a point or less, and 1 gets worse. It is not switched on yet, because for Argentina's yearly totals after 2021 it lands further from MODIS than the plain version (2022: plain within half a percent, smarter about 9% over), and we want to understand why first.

What you can open and try.

  • The web app, a burning calendar on a globe (https://dashboard.alexmong.com/spaceapps/explore.html). Turn the globe: each country is colored by its latest month against its usual. Click a country on the globe, or search the 235 listed countries and territories. You get the answer in words, the latest available month's hot spot detections against the historical median (the middle of the other years), and the burning calendar: as year lines (one line per year, one point per month) or as a grid (years down, months across, each month shaded against the same month in other years, with year totals). Switch between VIIRS's and MODIS's scale, and download the monthly table as a CSV file. It lists 235 countries and territories. Records begin in November 2000 where available and run as far as December 2025; Argentina has early data through November 12, 2026.
  • The main page (https://dashboard.alexmong.com/spaceapps/): the answer for the latest available month, the year so far, the last fire season or any past month; how we know; and the record: every year, this year, a world map of where the record holds up, and a sentence to copy into a report. The story told in our live talk is at https://dashboard.alexmong.com/spaceapps/#story/1.
  • The connector (https://dashboard.alexmong.com/spaceapps/connector.html). A small server that speaks the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the standard way an AI chat app plugs into a data source. Its eleven tools find a place, answer "is it burning more than usual?", compare two places or two periods, say how sure the record is, and write a sentence for a report. Ask "How bad were Australia's fires in December 2019?" and it reads all twenty-six Decembers and answers: about three times as many detections as a normal December. It can also read NASA's recent files, labeled 24 hours, 48 hours and seven days; those counts come straight from NASA and are not harmonized. On November 15, a command-line AI (OpenAI's Codex) used it to answer a question, calling three tools. Asked about the future, it gives the patterns to watch, never a forecast.
  • Fire, or something else? (https://dashboard.alexmong.com/spaceapps/volunteer/). Not every hot spot is a wildfire: some are factories, gas flares or volcanoes that stay hot all year. This volunteer page shows 50 real hot spots from 2020, half of them labeled fire by NASA. For each, you see pictures from space, the lights at night, a twelve-month heat record and the camera's heat readings, and you choose. NASA's own label is the answer key, shown after you pick.
  • Fire Detectives (https://dashboard.alexmong.com/spaceapps/fire-detectives/): lesson pages the team made to explain the two cameras to its children. Moe (MODIS) and Vee (VIIRS) started here.

What benefits does it have?

  • One consistent record. A change in camera no longer looks like a change in fire. Among the years we could compare, 63 of 65 busy countries show their biggest fire year after 2021 when the record is stitched together. On VIIRS's scale, 9 do: Brazil's biggest year goes back to 2007, India's to 2021, the United States' to 2005. Canada's 2023 stays its biggest year either way. One scale keeps a record that is really there.
  • It answers the challenge's own questions directly. Which months of the year burn most, which years had the most burning activity, and how a country's latest available month compares with the historical median.
  • It says how sure it is, place by place. Each country shows its test result where one is available, and thin records are labeled in plain words.
  • It lets big questions be asked fairly. Across a fixed set of 66 countries with complete records from 2003 to 2025, on one scale, the 2021 to 2025 average is about 14% below 2003 to 2007. That counts detections, not land burned, so it does not settle whether the world is burning less; it shows that the question can now be asked on one scale.
  • Light and open. The site is static files: your browser downloads small tables and does the math itself, so there is no database and nothing to install. The monthly tables download as CSV.
  • Several ways in. A globe for a person, a connector for an AI chat app, and a puzzle for volunteers, all built from NASA FIRMS data.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The challenge names early warning and emergency responders, scientists, land managers and firefighters. This record gives them a consistent fire history for an area of interest: when the critical period usually comes, which years were unusual, and whether the latest month is out of the ordinary, without the camera change pretending to be a fire trend. A land manager can see when a country's season usually peaks; a scientist can download the harmonized monthly table and start from one scale; a reporter or student can ask an AI chat app and get an answer drawn from NASA's data.

It is fire history to plan against, not a live map or a forecast; NASA itself advises against using these data for decisions on the ground.

What comes next: switch on the smarter fire-power version; add areas smaller than a country (drawing an area on a map, or typing latitude and longitude) and a from-to date range; offer a CSV of the hot spots themselves; save volunteers' picks so many eyes can help sort hot spots that are not fire; and ask an expert in satellite fire data to review the method. The volunteer page and the lesson pages also carry the project into classrooms and homes.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Data: NASA FIRMS active-fire hot spot files: MODIS (Collection 6.1) on Terra and Aqua, VIIRS (375 m) on Suomi NPP and NOAA-20.
  • Counting: Python 3.12 with DuckDB and PyArrow turn the raw files into small monthly tables for 235 countries and territories.
  • The harmonizing engine: one small file of plain JavaScript, the same file in the web page and in the connector.
  • The web app: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no framework, no build step and no outside library; the globe and the charts are drawn with SVG and the browser's canvas. Country outlines from Natural Earth. Fonts: Fredoka, Lexend and JetBrains Mono from Google Fonts.
  • The connector: Node.js with no outside packages, speaking the Model Context Protocol (JSON-RPC over HTTP).
  • The volunteer page: NASA GIBS pictures fetched live in the browser, plus stored 10 m close views and heat pictures made from Copernicus Sentinel-2 (found through the Earth Search catalog, cut with rasterio).
  • Hosting: one small Linux server (Ubuntu) running the Caddy web server.
  • Checks: Node.js scripts recompute the numbers shown on the main screens; a publish scan and a site self-test run before every copy to the server; headless Microsoft Edge takes pictures of each screen for review.
  • The talk: the team lead's recorded voice, cut with ffmpeg, with word times found by a speech-to-text model (faster-whisper, run on the laptop). QR codes made with the Python qrcode package and read back with OpenCV.
  • AI tools: Claude Code (Anthropic's Claude models) and the Codex command-line tool (OpenAI's models); ComfyUI for the Fire Detectives character art.
  • Hardware: a Windows laptop and one small Linux server.
  • The code is public at https://github.com/Alexander-Mong/two-cameras-one-calendar (Apache-2.0).

How is your project creative?

  • Two characters carry the science. Moe (MODIS, the older camera, drawn with glasses) and Vee (VIIRS, with sharper eyes) were hand-drawn by team members, and the whole family wrote and sang a song about the two cameras (words by a team member; music a traditional folk tune from Newfoundland, Canada). The song, to hear, read and download, is at https://dashboard.alexmong.com/spaceapps/song.html .
  • A conversion that shows its work. Seasonal numbers for each country where the data allow, tested on years left out, with each country's result shown where one is available.
  • A calendar you can turn in your hands. Each country's years recede like ridgelines beside a globe you spin, so the fire season shows as a shape you can see at once, and the grid is one click away for the exact counts.
  • The record answers in plain words, and answers an AI too. The same sentences reach a person on the web page and an AI chat app through the connector.
  • The question flipped into a puzzle. "Fire, or something else?" turns NASA's own labels into a game anyone can play, and teaches why a hot spot is not always a fire.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Honest units. Every count is a hot spot detection, never "fires" or land burned, and the page says so.
  • What to test against, and which scale to show. MODIS is the one camera with real counts in both eras, so the test translates into MODIS's terms. VIIRS is the camera going forward, so the calendar opens on VIIRS's scale, with a switch.
  • Seasons. One number for the whole year was wrong in most months, so every country whose data support it gets twelve; thinner records get a simpler conversion, and the page says which.
  • Plain and tested, before smarter. The plain version is the one switched on. The fire-power version is built and tested, and comes next.
  • Accessible colors. The calendar grid uses a single color ramp with the count printed in every cell, so it never relies on color alone.
  • People first. No forecasts and no safety advice; NASA's own caution about these data is on the page. The team's children are not named or shown in anything submitted.

The team, and SI in this project

Spark Squad is a homeschool family team: two parents and three children. The adults directed, reviewed and decided. AI coding assistants wrote the code. Team members hand-drew the two satellite characters and the scientist. The children read parts of the live talk, and the family wrote and sang the song.

SI (Super Intelligence) in this project: Claude models, through Claude Code, wrote the code, the analysis scripts and drafts of the text, under the team's direction. A second model family, OpenAI's, through the Codex command-line tool, independently recounted the main numbers and fact-checked the talk. Speech-to-text (Whisper) was used to cut the team lead's recorded voice; no AI voice is used in anything submitted. The Fire Detectives lesson pages use character art made with an AI image model, FLUX.2 klein 4B, run in ComfyUI, and each picture is marked as AI-generated. The idea of how to answer the challenge, and every decision, were the team's. No outside expert in satellite fire data has reviewed the work yet.
